title: Author the Tolerance Policy
subtitle: Write the rule that decides when a price gap is acceptable
scenario: It is 10:30 AM. The invoice bills $2.44; the PO agreed $2.40. Small gaps are normal - freight, rounding, minor repricing. But how small is small enough to pay without a human looking? That judgment cannot live in someone's head. Write it down as the Tolerance Policy the match will apply the same way every day.
input: Controller's guidance (v1.0.0, effective day-0): a line matches if the price variance is within the LARGER of 2% of the PO amount or $25.00. Received quantity must equal ordered quantity exactly (quantity tolerance 0). Anything outside these bounds is an exception for a human. Approved by the Controller.
instructions: Capture the policy version and its effective date.
Record the price tolerance as a percent and as an absolute dollar amount.
Record the quantity tolerance and who approved the policy.
Record the tolerance basis: which of the two price limits applies (the larger).
Return one valid JSON object. Use numbers for the tolerances.
copilotPrompt: Turn this tolerance guidance into a JSON policy record: version, priceTolerancePct, priceToleranceAbs, toleranceBasis (larger), qtyTolerance, approvedBy, effective. Use numbers for the tolerances.
successMessage: Tolerance Policy authored. The match now has one written rule to apply the same way every day.
editorHelper: Encode the Controller's rule as one JSON object the match can read.

intro.heading: Before you match: write the rule down

sections.title: Judgment becomes data
sections.body: Deciding when a price gap is acceptable is a policy. If it lives in a clerk's head it drifts; encoded as data, the match applies it identically every day and it can be audited.

sections.title: Two limits, take the larger
sections.body: The rule allows the LARGER of 2% of the PO or $25. On a small PO the dollar floor protects you; on a large PO the percent does. Recording the basis (larger) is as important as the numbers.

sections.title: Quantity is strict
sections.body: Price has tolerance; quantity does not. Received must equal ordered exactly (tolerance 0), because a quantity gap means goods are missing or over-shipped - never just rounding.

sections.title: Who owns it
sections.body: The Controller approves this policy. A version and effective date make it a controlled record - the match can cite exactly which rule it applied.

fieldGuide.meaning: The policy version, so the match can cite which rule it applied.
fieldGuide.hint: The semantic version stated in the guidance.

fieldGuide.meaning: Allowed price variance as a percent of the PO amount.
fieldGuide.hint: The percent figure - store the number 2, not '2%'.

fieldGuide.meaning: Allowed price variance as an absolute dollar amount.
fieldGuide.hint: The absolute dollar limit - store 25, not '$25.00'.

fieldGuide.meaning: Which of the two limits applies when they differ.
fieldGuide.lookFor: larger or smaller of the two?
fieldGuide.hint: The rule says use the LARGER of the percent or the absolute.

fieldGuide.meaning: Allowed difference between received and ordered quantity.
fieldGuide.hint: Quantity must match exactly - the tolerance is 0.

fieldGuide.meaning: The role that approved this policy.
fieldGuide.hint: The role named as approving the guidance.
The effective date stated in the guidance.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd write the match tolerances down (e.g. 'price within 2%, quantity exact') in a config tab so the match check uses one agreed rule set.

bestFit.how: Environment Variables or a config list holding the tolerance limits, owned by the Controller
a config dict with a version and an effective date, so an old run can be re-explained
a data store record read at the top of the scenario rather than a number typed into a filter

takeaway.heading: Tolerance Policy authored
points: You turned the Controller's judgment into a written, versioned rule the match applies the same way every day.
The price limit is the LARGER of 2% or $25 - recording the basis matters as much as the two numbers.
Quantity tolerance is 0: received must equal ordered exactly, because a quantity gap is never just rounding.
The policy is saved as tolerance-policy.json with an approver and effective date - a controlled, auditable record.
The workflow can now decide when a price gap is acceptable without a human judging each one.
